title: Identifiability through GPS and timestamp data

title: Excessive data collection beyond necessity

assumptions: The device collects all sensor data regardless of whether it's needed for the specific use case.

title: Usurpation of user identity through device data

title: Linkability of manual health entries across time and contexts
description: User's manually logged calorie, meal, and weight data could be linked across multiple sessions to create a detailed health profile, potentially revealing patterns about lifestyle, health conditions, or daily routines.
assumptions: Data is stored persistently and accessible for analysis over time

title: Identifiability through unique health data patterns
description: The combination of specific weight entries, meal logs, and calorie data could potentially identify the user, especially if the data is unique or combined with other information sources.
assumptions: Health data patterns are distinctive enough to identify individuals

title: Disclosure of sensitive health data to unauthorized parties
description: The companion app could disclose the user's manually entered health data (weight, meals, calories) to third parties through data breaches, improper sharing, or unauthorized access.
assumptions: App has access to third-party services or APIs that could leak data

title: Unawareness of data usage and sharing

title: Explicit Location Data Disclosure to Data Store
description: GPS location traces with timestamps are explicitly written to the location history store, constituting a designed transfer of highly sensitive personal data. This disclosure is avoidable if the data were not required for the app's core functionality, or if it could be anonymized/pseudonymized before storage.
assumptions: The app has legitimate need to store location history, but the minimality principle should be applied.

title: Identifiability of Location Traces
description: GPS location data with timestamps is inherently identifiable to specific individuals. Even without explicit identifiers, movement patterns can uniquely identify users and their routines, habits, and locations.
assumptions: Location data can be correlated with user identity through device identifiers or other metadata.

title: Linkability of Location Data Across Time
description: Location traces can be linked across different time periods to create comprehensive movement profiles, potentially revealing sensitive information about user behavior, relationships, and routines that were not intended to be disclosed.
assumptions: Location data can be correlated with other data sources or time periods to build detailed user profiles.

title: Data Integrity Compromise of Location History
description: Location data stored in the data store could be altered, deleted, or tampered with by unauthorized parties or through system failures, compromising the accuracy and reliability of the stored location history.
assumptions: The data store has appropriate access controls and integrity mechanisms in place.

title: Explicit Health Data Disclosure to Analytics Service
description: Health log data (calorie, weight, exercise logs) is explicitly transferred from the Health Log Store to the Health Analytics Service for health-condition analysis. This represents an intentional disclosure of personal health data across the DataStore→Process boundary.
assumptions: The analytics service is authorized to access this data for its intended purpose.

title: Data Store Unavailability for Health Log Access
description: The Health Log Store may become unavailable, preventing the Analytics Service from accessing historical health logs needed for health-condition analysis.
assumptions: No redundancy or failover mechanisms exist for the data store.
uncertainty_note: Context does not specify availability controls for this flow.

title: Location History Data Disclosure to Analytics Service
description: The Location History Store (DS2) transfers sensitive location data to the Health Analytics Service (P3) for pattern analysis. This explicit disclosure of personal location data across a system boundary may reveal sensitive information about daily routines, movement patterns, and potentially health-related behaviors. The minimality principle is at risk as the system may collect and transfer more location data than strictly necessary for the analytics purpose.
assumptions: The analytics service has legitimate access to location data for deriving daily routine patterns, but the scope of data transfer may exceed what's minimally required.
uncertainty_note: Tree node Dd.1.1 is inferred from context about data disclosure; exact LINDDUN Pro node may vary.

title: Implicit Disclosure of Sensitive Patterns from Location Analysis
description: The Health Analytics Service (P3) processes location history to derive daily routine and movement patterns. This processing may result in implicit disclosure of sensitive personal information (e.g., health conditions, religious practices, political activities, or sensitive locations) through derived patterns, even if raw location data is not directly exposed.
assumptions: Pattern analysis can infer sensitive activities from location data alone, creating implicit disclosure risks beyond the explicit data transfer.

title: Profiling via inferred health insights
description: Inferred health analytics insights (risk indicators, trend flags) about one individual may reveal information about a larger group of individuals through known relations or similarity, enabling profiling beyond the intended scope.
assumptions: The app or third parties can correlate individual insights with group-level health patterns.
uncertainty_note: Citation L.2.2.2 from context is approximate - this is a reasonable application of the profiling concept to health analytics.

title: Identity inference from health analytics
description: Inferred health-condition risk indicators and trend flags may be combined with other data to identify the data subject, especially if the insights are distinctive enough to narrow down to specific individuals.
assumptions: The app or external parties have access to additional identifying information that can be correlated with the analytics insights.
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is inferred from general LINDDUN methodology - context didn't provide specific I-tree nodes.

title: Insufficient cybersecurity risk management for health analytics
description: The Health Analytics Service may lack proper cybersecurity risk management controls, creating gaps that expose privacy risks when transmitting sensitive inferred health insights to the mobile app.
assumptions: Health data handling requires strict cybersecurity measures under regulations like HIPAA/GDPR; inadequate controls constitute non-compliance.

title: Unauthorized disclosure of health condition indicators
description: The app dashboard displays sensitive health condition indicators (eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals) to the user. If the app has vulnerabilities or if the user shares this information with third parties, the data could be disclosed to unauthorized parties beyond the intended recipient.
assumptions: The app may have security vulnerabilities or the user may share sensitive health information with others.

title: User unawareness of data implications
description: Users may not fully understand the implications of displaying health condition indicators, including potential consequences of sharing this information, data retention policies, or how the indicators are inferred.

title: Non-compliance with health data regulations
description: Displaying health condition indicators may raise compliance issues with regulations such as HIPAA, GDPR, or other health data protection laws. The app may not have proper consent mechanisms, data minimization, or user rights management for health-related data.
assumptions: Health data displays may trigger regulatory requirements that are not fully addressed in the app's design.

title: Explicit Data Disclosure to Third-Party Cloud Provider
description: Health analytics data, models, and full health and location dataset are explicitly transferred to and hosted at external cloud provider EE2. This represents intentional disclosure of sensitive personal data across system boundary.
assumptions: Cloud provider EE2 has access to all health and location data; data is replicated at EE2's infrastructure

title: Implicit Data Disclosure via Metadata
description: Metadata about health data access patterns, query frequencies, or model usage at EE2 could be inferred and disclosed, revealing information about system usage even if raw data is protected.
assumptions: Cloud provider may log access patterns, query metadata, or usage statistics
uncertainty_note: Depends on EE2's logging and monitoring practices

title: Linkability of Health Data at Cloud Provider
description: Health and location data hosted at EE2 could potentially be linked with other datasets (e.g., if EE2 hosts other services or if data is re-identified through cross-referencing with public records).
assumptions: EE2 may have access to other data sources; location data combined with health data increases re-identification risk
uncertainty_note: Depends on EE2's data isolation policies and what other data they host

title: Re-identification Risk of Health and Location Data
description: Full health and location dataset at EE2 may allow re-identification of individuals, especially when location data is combined with health records, creating unique identifiers.
assumptions: Location data combined with health data creates quasi-identifiers; health data is inherently sensitive
uncertainty_note: Depends on data granularity and whether anonymization was applied before transfer

title: Unauthorized Access to Hosted Health Data
description: Health and location data at EE2 may be accessible to unauthorized parties including EE2 employees, other EE2 customers, or through security breaches at the cloud provider.
assumptions: EE2 has multiple tenants or employees; cloud infrastructure may have vulnerabilities
uncertainty_note: Depends on EE2's security controls, tenant isolation, and access management

title: Data Integrity Compromise at Cloud Provider
description: Health and location data hosted at EE2 could be tampered with, corrupted, or altered by malicious actors or through system failures at the cloud provider.
assumptions: EE2 infrastructure may be vulnerable to attacks; data replication could introduce inconsistencies
uncertainty_note: Depends on EE2's security measures and data integrity controls

title: Non-compliance with Data Protection Regulations
description: Transfer of health and location data to EE2 may violate GDPR, HIPAA, or other data protection regulations if proper safeguards, consent, or data processing agreements are not in place.
assumptions: Health data is regulated; cross-border or third-party data transfer requires compliance measures
uncertainty_note: Depends on EE2's location, certifications, and contractual agreements
